slides.title: ASENA
slides.script:
I’ll talk about two recent projects on code as policy for robotics.
The first is ASENA, which focuses on navigation. We connect a coding agent to a robot environment and explore recursive self-improvement, or RSI.
The second is Recova, which focuses on manipulation with recovery skills. Here, we use code as policy to improve learned robot policies. The goal is to make the whole loop of data collection, training, and deployment as autonomous as possible.

slides.title: The agent composes, the robot executes
slides.script: Basically, we give a coding agent a task and observations, from either a real robot or a simulator. It writes code to control the robot, using two kinds of tools: learned policies, like VLN, and interfaces to cameras, LiDAR, and robot control. Then it looks at what happened and tries the next step.

slides.title: Parallel workers evolve a shared workspace
slides.script:
In each pass, the agent writes code to solve the tasks. We keep the useful code as skills for the next round. The model weights stay fixed.
To scale this up, we need to collect those rollouts efficiently. So we use 16 parallel workers, each with its own simulation environment and private workspace, plus access to the navigation policy.
We distribute the tasks across the workers. After each pass, an improver agent merges, tests, and prunes their updates. That improved workspace becomes the starting point for the next pass.
This is also ready to use as a rollout environment for code-as-policy training.

slides.title: The sandbox limits what generated code can do
slides.script:
The workspace is a sandbox. The agent can write code and notes, but it can’t change the platform or access operator credentials.

On the real robot, we’re more strict. A motion proposal goes through validation, then operator approval, before we send it to SONIC.

This sandbox can also support agent training.

slides.title: The interaction layer can support an agent-training loop
slides.script:
Here, we’re making a connection between RSI and agent training, which is our future work.

For RSI, we keep the model fixed and improve the skills. For training, we could swap the API for a trainable model and use the same environments for rollouts. The goal is to make the coding agent faster.

slides.title: ASENA-VLN provides reusable navigation
slides.script:
We also developed a navigation policy called ASENA-VLN. On its own, it achieves state-of-the-art success on R2R. I won’t go into the policy details here.

What’s more interesting is what happens when a coding agent calls this policy.

slides.title: The navigation tool reduces coding-agent interaction
slides.script: Adding VLN helps some models more than others. Claude goes up eleven points, while Astra goes down seven. But both use far fewer tool calls. So the learned policy still helps a lot with efficiency.

slides.title: Success grows as the workspace accumulates experience
slides.script: This is one of the most exciting results we saw from RSI. As we run more passes and improve the workspace, success on these recurring R2R tasks reaches 98%—with the model weights completely fixed.

slides.title: Real runs leave records we can inspect and reuse
slides.script: Finally, we record observations, robot states, actions, code, and feedback from real-world runs, giving model teams rich multimodal data that could support future training of both robot policies and frontier models.
